summary: Teaching 8–9-year-olds to read and interpret food web diagrams. The concept of feeding relationships is already known; the new learning is decoding the diagram convention — above all the arrow-direction rule: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, in the direction energy/matter flows. Learners name producers vs consumers, trace a single chain through the tangle, find organisms shared by several chains, and predict knock-on effects of removing a species. Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; complexity should come from interconnection, not unfamiliar species.
misconceptions: Drawing/reading the arrow backwards — pointing from the eater to the food (thinking the arrow means 'eats') rather than in the direction energy flows.
Believing a web is just one long chain, so removing an organism only affects the next one along, not every path it feeds.
Thinking arrows show 'who is bigger/stronger' rather than what eats what.
Assuming an organism can only be in one chain, missing that many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains.

activities.title: Lock in the arrow-direction rule first
steps: Look at a single arrow between two pictured organisms, e.g. grass → rabbit, and say exactly what it means: the arrow points to the eater, so energy/matter flows FROM grass TO rabbit.
Given 'a caterpillar and a bird that eats it', draw the arrow yourself, pointing the right way (caterpillar → bird).
Check every arrowhead in a small web points toward the feeder, re-reading each as 'is eaten by / energy goes to'.

Redraw a three-species chain with all its arrows reversed and decide whether it still makes sense — it does not, because energy would then appear to flow from the eater back to its food, the opposite of how feeding works.
activities.insight: The arrowhead carries the meaning: it shows the direction energy/matter travels, from food to feeder — not 'this eats that'.

activities.title: Build the web up from chains and name the roles
steps: Start from one chain you can already read (grass → rabbit → fox); then overlay a second and third chain that share an organism, so the web grows from chains rather than appearing as a full tangle.

Name each organism's role: producers (plants, which make their own food using sunlight) and consumers; then split the consumers into primary consumers (eat producers) and secondary consumers (eat other consumers). If decomposers (e.g. fungi, worms, bacteria) are shown, name them as feeders on dead material and waste. Notice that a producer has no food arrows arriving at it, but check that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn in the web would also have only arrows leaving it.
Trace one chain end-to-end with a finger, saying the running label aloud (grass → rabbit → fox).
activities.insight: A food web is many overlapping chains, and each organism plays a role (producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, or decomposer if shown) that you can read from the diagram.

activities.title: Find shared organisms at crossing points
steps: Trace two different food chains that both pass through the same animal in the web.
Highlight one organism and follow every arrow that touches it to see how many chains cross there.
activities.insight: Many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains — a web is a mesh, not a set of separate lines.

activities.title: Predict the ripple when a species is removed
steps: Pick an organism (e.g. rabbits) and, following the arrows, predict whose food disappears if it is removed.
Trace along every path the removed organism fed — not just the next one along — and name each organism affected downstream.
Explain to a partner or an 'ecologist' character why removing one node can affect more than one other animal.
activities.insight: Removing one node ripples along EVERY path it fed: because a web is interconnected, one removal can affect several organisms, not just the next one in a single chain.

activities.title: Optional interactive web-reader and companion reference
steps: On an interactive pictured web of 6–8 familiar organisms (grass, rabbit, mouse, fox, owl, beetle, hawk), tap an organism so every arrow it touches lights up, revealing the mesh of relationships.
Drag a fingertip from grass through rabbit to fox to trace a single chain, with a running 'grass → rabbit → fox' label naming it.

Press a 'remove' button on an organism and watch the arrows leaving it dim and the organisms that fed on it (e.g. fox AND owl after removing the rabbit) light up as losing one food source. They do not automatically disappear if the web shows they have other food (e.g. a fox that also eats mice).

As a pre-teach reference, use a static annotated web with lift-the-flaps: tap each arrow to reveal 'the arrow points to the eater — energy flows this way', tap each node to reveal its producer/predator/prey role.
activities.insight: Interactive highlighting, tracing, and a visible removal-ripple can make the mesh structure and the knock-on effects of removal concrete and felt.

checkQuestion: Show a food web diagram. First: 'Point to one arrow and tell me exactly what it means — which way does the food and energy travel along it?' Then: 'Now I name two animals — a caterpillar and a bird that eats it. Draw the arrow between them yourself, pointing the right way.'
checkAnswer: The arrow means 'is eaten by' — energy travels in the direction of the arrowhead, from the food to the feeder. The drawn arrow therefore goes FROM the caterpillar TO the bird (caterpillar → bird).
